title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) to quantify the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic verifier (+optional repair) between an LLM generator and network change application. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 paired intent→configuration tasks and ran a single shared generator output per task (gpt-5-mini requested). The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded − baseline). Observed outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies, guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10k resamples, seed=1729) 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00]. The repair pathway was never invoked (repair_applied == false for all pairs). We release the full preregistration, provider/model traces, validator traces, deterministic reconciliation, and analysis artifacts (see Disclosure) so others can replay and extend the design. We interpret the null as a ceiling effect under the chosen task/model/validator conditions and discuss implications for future designs that aim to demonstrate verifier/repair utility.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation could materially reduce operator workload in NetOps, but unsafe proposals risk outages. The generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) architecture—where a verifier checks LLM proposals and a repair step is optionally invoked—has been proposed as a practical guardrail. Prior work (e.g., Cornetto and related generate‑validate‑repair studies) documents settings where verification reduces regressions, but real operational value depends on the joint distribution of generator errors and validator coverage. To obtain an unbiased estimate of the verifier’s marginal contribution we preregistered a paired confirmatory protocol that holds the generator output fixed and compares the binary apply outcome with and without the verifier+repair layer. Our preregistered research question: To what extent does an iterative G→V→R pipeline reduce regression‑causing network changes compared to an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline, under a paired design and deterministic task pool? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired evaluation (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) with deterministic sampling and immutable hashes; (2) a transparent null result (K=200) with exact statistical inference and full archival; (3) diagnostics and operational lessons for future confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: Work on LLM‑assisted NetOps and AIOps spans intent translation, retrieval‑augmented generation, and verifier‑guided repair loops. Cornetto (Protogeros et al., 2026) proposes a large synthetic benchmark to assess LLM repair of network configurations and reports that verification reduces regressions in many generator/scale regimes. Other recent contributions (e.g., TypoNet, self‑evolving verifiers) argue for constraining LLMs to translation tasks while delegating reasoning to verifiers/solvers; survey coverage and evaluation recommendations emphasize workflow‑centred measures over static QA metrics. Our design differs by isolating the verifier’s marginal effect via a paired shared‑initial generation: rather than comparing distinct generator runs, we apply a single generator output to both arms so any difference can only arise from verification/repair. This isolates the verifier role but does not measure interactive generator–verifier feedback loops that agentic workflows may exploit.
sections.methodology: Preregistration. The full preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) froze the research question, sampling, inclusion rules, validator identity, model request, maximum call budget, repair policy, primary estimand, statistical test, and bootstrap settings. Preregistration SHA‑256: a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622 (artifact archived). Design (paired shared_generation). For each intent we produced exactly one generator output (shared_initial_generation). That same candidate was evaluated in both arms: baseline (LLM proposal accepted and scored) and guarded (deterministic validator runs; if invalid the preregistered guarded policy allowed one repair call). This holds generator variability constant and isolates verifier/repair marginal effect. Task sampling. Tasks were deterministically drawn from the public synthetic pool implemented by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5, filtered to those covered by deterministic_netops_validator_v5, hashed (SHA‑256(intent_string)), sorted, and the first K=200 selected. This deterministic selection and automated exclusions (none in this run) are logged at execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256: f1d447b7...). Validator, scoring rules, repair policy. Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (scorer_id). Scoring rule for the primary outcome: full_intent_constraint_validation (validator returns valid boolean, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, normalized_configuration, violation codes). Repair policy: maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 (preregistered). Model and provider. Requested model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Execution budget: maximum_model_calls = 400 (one shared generation per task used 200 total calls). Implementation and provenance. All raw responses, provider traces, and validator outputs were persisted and SHA‑256 hashed. Representative files and hashes: raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 3dfbe1b6...), transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256: 79c91155...), provider call traces execution/provider_calls/*.json, scoring traces execution/scoring/*.json, responses execution/responses/*.txt. The initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Statistical analysis. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confirmatory test: exact McNemar two‑sided test. Bootstrap: percentile bootstrap, 10,000 resamples, seed=1729 (preregistered). Missingness/exclusions. The preregistered rule was to exclude pairs only when both arms produced unrecoverable apply failures; no human adjudication was permitted. All exclusion decisions and missingness are logged; for this run none occurred.

sections.discussion:
Why a null result occurred. The paired shared_initial_generation design intentionally isolates the verifier’s marginal effect by eliminating generator variability. In this constrained regime the generator proposals satisfied the validator constraints for every sampled intent, producing a ceiling effect: there was no opportunity for the verifier to block or for repair to change the binary apply outcome. This outcome is internally valid and fully logged, but it does not contradict prior studies that observed verifier benefits in error‑rich generator settings; it instead clarifies the boundary condition where verifier marginal value is null.
Implications for evaluation design. To demonstrate verifier/repair utility in confirmatory settings future experiments should ensure baseline generator error is nontrivial. Practical options (all compatible with our archival approach) include: (1) sample tasks near the validator coverage boundary or deliberately include intents outside coverage; (2) use generator variants (smaller models or temperature increases) to raise baseline error rates; (3) enable the generator to receive verifier feedback (interactive loop) so the downstream behavior differs between arms; or (4) stress test with adversarially perturbed proposals. Each option alters estimands and operational realism; we provide our artifacts so others can replay and compare alternative designs deterministically.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired comparison of a G→V→R pipeline against an LLM‑only pipeline on a deterministic synthetic NetOps task pool. Under the preregistered contract (shared generator output; deterministic validator/coverage), both arms yielded 200/200 validator‑compliant applies and the observed paired difference was exactly zero (McNemar p=1.00; bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00]). The repair loop never executed. The run documents a ceiling case and highlights that demonstrating verifier value requires a design that exposes generator failures or allows generator–verifier interactions. We publish the complete artifact bundle and hash manifests to support exact replay and methodical follow‑on studies.

limitations: Single requested model (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without further experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool with deterministic sampling and explicit validator coverage — external validity to production intents and natural operator distributions is limited.
Primary outcome measures validator conformity (validator.valid); construct validity depends on fidelity and coverage of deterministic_netops_validator_v5.
Ceiling effect: observed baseline success = 100% removed the possibility of observing verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (model pretraining overlap with task texts) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items in this run.
